topic: The DNA of Space: From Linear Combinations to Bases
target_audience: First-year university students or advanced high school students learning Linear Algebra.

sections.title: Prerequisites: Vectors as Directions
sections.content: Briefly revisit vectors as 'movement instructions' rather than just points. Establish the operations of scaling (stretching) and addition (tip-to-tail).
sections.example: Imagine a Robot Scout. Vector v1 is '1 step North' and v2 is '1 step East'. Scaling 2*v1 means taking 2 steps North.

sections.title: Linear Combinations: The Vector Recipe
sections.content: Define a linear combination as the result of scaling vectors and adding them together (a*v + b*w). Visually show the 'tip-to-tail' method on a 2D grid.
sections.example: To reach a hidden treasure at (3, 2), our Robot uses a 'recipe': 3*(1 step East) + 2*(1 step North). This sum is a linear combination of the East and North vectors.

sections.title: Span: The Reachable Map
sections.content: Introduce 'Span' as the set of all possible linear combinations of a group of vectors. Use animation to show a line or plane being 'painted' as scalars vary from negative to positive infinity.
sections.example: If the Robot only has one vector (East), its 'Span' is a single horizontal line. If it has East and North, its 'Span' is the entire 2D flat floor.

sections.title: Linear Dependence: The Redundant Helper
sections.content: Explain linear dependence as 'redundancy.' If one vector can already be reached using the others (it's already in their span), it is dependent. Visually, show a third vector lying exactly on the plane created by two others.
sections.example: Suppose the Robot has three movement vectors: North, East, and North-East. The 'North-East' vector is redundant because the Robot could already reach any point using just North and East. These three are 'Linearly Dependent'.

sections.title: The Basis: The Efficient Toolkit
sections.content: Define a 'Basis' as a set of vectors that are both linearly independent (no redundancy) and span the entire space (can reach everywhere). It is the 'minimalist' set of instructions for a dimension.
sections.example: For a 2D map, {North, East} is a basis. {North, East, North-East} is not (redundant). {North} is not (cannot reach East). A Basis is like a 'Standard Unit' that defines the grid.
